Before even trying to have a child, my wife and I already knew many parents. Now I know that quite a few of them were tremendously happy. Back then it was not very noticeable.

They told us about not sleeping, the logistics, the endless illnesses, how hard it was to travel and how little a Sunday with children looked like a Sunday without them. All of that was true. What they almost never said with the same clarity was something much simpler: having children had made them happy.

Happiness appeared in photos, maybe, but rarely in conversation. It always arrived surrounded by precautions. «It is the best thing that has happened to me, but...». After the *but* came a list of sacrifices long enough to neutralize any chance that it sounded like a recommendation.

TV shows did not help much either. In many of them, children are the force that turns adult life into a succession of sleep, diapers, arguments and lost opportunities. When the story wants to represent freedom, its characters travel, change jobs, fall in love or start over. When it wants to represent that real life has arrived, a baby appears and the music stops.

Now that Esteban is five months old I begin to understand why we parents speak like this.

Telling someone that having a child has made you tremendously happy is delicate. You do not know if they want to have them, if they can, if they are trying without success or if they just decided that this life is not for them. You also do not want to turn a personal experience into a doctrine or look like one of those converts who, as soon as they discover something, need to recruit the rest.

So you learn to start with the difficulties. It is a kind of liability waiver: before saying you are happy, you prove that you are also tired and that you perfectly understand the price you have paid.

Then there is work. In certain professional environments, speaking with too much enthusiasm about fatherhood can sound like a confession of low ambition. It seems more serious to say that your company, your career or the next project occupy the center of your life. Saying that a child now occupies a large part of it can be interpreted as slowing down.

In the case of women, that suspicion has much more real and unfair consequences. We men can be celebrated for being involved fathers; mothers are still asked, although not always out loud, how much professional commitment they might have lost. It is not strange that many people protect their image of ambition by keeping family happiness in a discreet background.

And then there is the *Zeitgeist*. Boasting about a company, a trip, a house or having run a marathon is perfectly acceptable. Saying that having a child is one of the happiest and most meaningful experiences you have lived sounds conventional, unsophisticated or even suspiciously defensive. As if only someone who needs to justify the loss of their old freedom could say it.

Complaining, on the other hand, is allowed. A father can say he has not slept for six months and nobody thinks he is exaggerating. If he says he had never been so happy, it seems he is romanticizing fatherhood.

The result is a half-told truth.

I have only been a father for five months. I am perfectly aware that I am missing almost all the difficult stages and that it would be ridiculous to present myself as an authority. We have already slept little, argued about absurd things and discovered that leaving the house can require logistical planning comparable to moving. I feel no need to hide that part.

But I can also say that my wife and I are tremendously happy. Not happy every minute nor protected from worry, exhaustion or fear. Happy to have had Esteban. Happy in a new way, quite hard to explain from the outside and much easier to recognize once you are inside.

My impression, limited to the people I know, is that something similar happens to the vast majority of parents. They can be exhausted, have relationship problems, feel overwhelmed or miss parts of their previous life. None of that prevents them from being deeply happy that their children exist. Daily difficulty and satisfaction with the decision are not opposite extremes.

I think this remains true even for many divorced parents where childcare had a major weight in their breakup. The lack of sleep, the unequal division of tasks, the disappearance of couple time or differences on how to raise children can wear down a relationship until it breaks. Even so, if they could go back and keep the marriage in exchange for their children not existing, I suspect almost none would accept the deal.

It is an impossible counterfactual and I cannot know what each person would choose. But I think most would be much more miserable without their children, even if being parents contributed to another important part of their life going wrong. An experience can worsen one dimension of life and, at the same time, make the whole life much more worthwhile.

Part of that happiness may come from something quite simple: caring for another person and being, for many years, the most useful person in the world for them offers a very easy compass to follow. A child needs you to feed them, comfort them, protect them and teach them to live. The specific tasks can be exhausting, but you rarely have to ask yourself why they matter.

It is a much clearer way to give meaning to life than pursuing a successful professional career, traveling the world or accumulating any of the experiences we usually present as the great reward of adult freedom. There is nothing wrong with those things. I have dedicated a huge part of my life to my work, I love traveling and I have no intention of giving up either completely. But they are much harder compasses to read: there is always a better job, a bigger company, another country and a new experience you have not lived yet.

Having a child reduces some options, but greatly increases clarity. You no longer have to build from scratch an explanation of what each day is for. There is a specific person whose life is better because you are there. You partially give up some clichés of the interesting life and discover another one that, precisely because it is so old and so common, we had perhaps stopped taking seriously.

I think we parents hide this happiness for good reasons: caution, respect, fear of boasting, awareness that there is no universal experience. But maybe that caution has a cost.

Many thirty-somethings in my circle have had children after thirty-five. It would be frivolous to attribute this mainly to a matter of narrative. Economic uncertainty, job insecurity, housing, the difficulty of balancing work and life, and finding a partner later weigh much more. Nothing is fixed by telling someone they should have had children earlier when they had no stability to care for them.

But I do not think those are the only reasons.

For years we have received a detailed description of everything you lose when having children and a much more timid explanation of what you gain. We have heard about freedom, sleep, money, travel, sex, career and personal time. Much less about the joy, the love, the sense of purpose or the strange expansion of life that can come from caring for someone.

If you only know the costs well, it is logical to postpone the decision until you feel completely ready. The problem is that this moment may never arrive and biology does not adapt very well to our professional calendars. Some decisions allow decades of rehearsal. This one does not always.

I am not saying everyone should have children. There are people who know they do not want them and build magnificent lives. There are others who want them and cannot have them, or for whom the path involves a pain that those of us who have been lucky can barely imagine. Fatherhood does not grant moral superiority, it does not automatically fix a life and it does not guarantee happiness.

I also do not think we should dedicate ourselves to convincing our friends. Selling fatherhood better does not mean recruiting. It means telling the complete experience.

Maybe it is enough to say both truths in the same sentence: it is very difficult and it has made me tremendously happy.

Before having Esteban I would have liked to hear that sentence without it being immediately disabled by ten warnings. I do not know if we would have decided to have him earlier. Important decisions never depend on a single cause and it is very easy to rewrite the past from the calm of the present. But at least we would have had information that now seems essential to me.

I understand my friends were cautious. Maybe they were trying not to pressure us, not to hurt us or not to seem less ambitious. Maybe they thought happiness was visible and did not need to be named.

I think it does need to be named.

Not so that everyone chooses the same life, but so that those who are trying to imagine it do not only receive the inventory of sacrifices. We parents are terrible at selling having children because we explain the price very well and almost whisper what makes us willing to pay it again.

Llevo escribiendo en internet desde 2004. Tenía catorce años y empecé con un blog sobre mi instituto, que a esa edad era casi lo mismo que hacer un blog sobre el mundo entero.

Con los años cambiaron los temas y los sitios, pero no demasiado la motivación. Escribí sobre fotografía en Xataka Foto. Después tuve un fotoblog en El País. Todo aquello ocurrió mientras estaba en la universidad. Más tarde publiqué algún artículo suelto en Medium, pero durante mucho tiempo mi verdadero blog fue Twitter: miles de ideas partidas en trozos cada vez más pequeños, hasta reunir a más de 30.000 personas al otro lado.

Ahora lo veo bastante claro: siempre escribí para que alguien hiciera algo.

Quería que me leyeran, por supuesto, pero no por una noble vocación de contribuir a la conversación pública. Escribía porque necesitaba ligar, ganar dinero y hacer amigos. Podría ennoblecer aquellos motivos ahora, pero la verdad es esa. Y también es verdad que conseguí las tres cosas.

Escribir públicamente me llevó, de manera directa o indirecta, a conocer a mi mujer, a muchos de mis mejores amigos actuales y prácticamente a cada una de las decenas de personas que he contratado durante estos años en Graphext. Visto así, escribir en internet no ha sido un accesorio de mi vida adulta. Ha sido una de sus infraestructuras invisibles.

Había además otra motivación, algo más difícil de explicar: escribía para obligarme a tener una vida más interesante. Si uno quiere tener algo que contar, tiene que prestar más atención, moverse y salir a buscarlo. Un blog era una especie de contrato con la versión de mí mismo que quería ser. Primero construyes un personaje; después intentas vivir a su altura.

Creo que funcionó. No sé cuántas cosas hice porque realmente quería hacerlas y cuántas porque intuía que algún día podría contarlas. Probablemente la diferencia no importe demasiado. El relato también empujó la vida.

Escribía hacia fuera. Y eso me obligaba a vivir hacia fuera.

Ahora tengo treinta y seis años. Estoy casado, Esteban nació hace cinco meses y profesionalmente me va muy bien. No significa que ya no quiera gustar, ganar más dinero o conocer a gente interesante. Significa que aquel motor ya no tira de mí con la misma fuerza. Por primera vez, volver a escribir no responde a una estrategia ni a una necesidad urgente de que ocurra algo al otro lado de la pantalla.

Quiero escribir para poder leerme cuando tenga setenta años.

Escribir para ese lector futuro resuelve además un problema que noto cada vez más conforme me hago mayor. Muchas veces descarto una idea antes de escribirla porque no me parece demasiado original. Seguro que alguien ya la ha pensado, la ha explicado mejor y ha escrito un libro sobre ella. Entonces decido que no merece la pena añadir otra versión peor a internet.

Me pasa algo parecido con el cine. Tengo la sensación de haber visto ya todos los tropos narrativos de todas las películas. Aparece un personaje y creo saber qué arco tendrá. Empieza una escena y enseguida recuerdo otras de las que parece descender. Acumular referencias ayuda a entender mejor las cosas, pero también puede convertirse en una máquina de quitarles valor: como reconozco los ingredientes, doy por hecho que el plato ya no puede sorprenderme.

Si escribo para mí, la originalidad deja de ser el precio de entrada. Al hombre de setenta años que lea esto no le importará si el de treinta y seis fue el primero en pensar una idea. Querrá saber cuáles le importaban, cómo llegó hasta ellas y qué hizo con ellas. Un pensamiento no tiene que ser inédito para merecer ser conservado. Basta con que sea realmente mío en este momento.

Eso me devuelve una motivación para escribir que había ido perdiendo: no tengo que aportar una gran idea nueva cada vez que publico. Puedo intentar entender por mi cuenta una idea vieja. Dentro de treinta años, lo valioso no será haber sido original, sino haber dejado un rastro honesto.

Eso no convierte un blog público en un diario privado. Al hacerme mayor he aprendido que no todo lo que me pasa me pertenece por completo. Una discusión familiar, el mal momento de un amigo o una tensión con un compañero de trabajo forman parte de mi vida, pero también de la suya. Ellos no han elegido convertirse en personajes secundarios de mi historia.

Por eso ahora valoro mucho más la autocensura. La palabra tiene mala fama porque suena a miedo o falta de sinceridad, pero a veces es una forma de cuidado y de lealtad. En el calor de un momento, una intimidad transitoria puede parecer esencial para explicar lo que uno siente. Unos meses después quizá se haya resuelto, haya perdido toda importancia o descubramos que la contamos de una forma profundamente injusta. El texto publicado, sin embargo, permanece.

Pienso, por ejemplo, en el suicidio de un amigo. Creo que a él no le habría importado que escribiera sobre ello. Pero la historia de su muerte no le pertenece solo a él y, desde luego, no me pertenece solo a mí. También forma parte del duelo y de la intimidad de su familia y de los amigos que lo quisieron. Contarla podría ayudarme a ordenar lo que sentí; publicarla podría obligarlos a encontrarse con una versión de algo que quizá prefieran vivir fuera de internet.

Ahí está la diferencia entre escribir y publicar. Puedo necesitar escribir una historia sin tener por ello derecho a compartirla.

Ser honesto sobre lo que pienso no me da derecho a exponer la intimidad de mi familia, mis amigos o mis compañeros de trabajo. Quiero escribir con suficiente profundidad como para conservar mi pensamiento, pero también con suficiente prudencia como para no fijar a los demás en un momento que solo era pasajero. Hay silencios que no son cobardía. Son afecto.

Los textos que escribí hace veinte años me conmueven de una manera que no consiguen las fotografías, los vídeos o los tuits de entonces. Una foto conserva lo que tenía delante. Un vídeo guarda cómo nos movíamos y cómo sonaba nuestra voz. Un tuit conserva una ocurrencia o una reacción. Pero un texto largo guarda algo distinto: el recorrido que hacía mi cabeza para llegar de una idea a otra.

Muchos de aquellos textos me parecen ingenuos. Algunos están mal escritos. En otros descubro a alguien demasiado seguro de cosas que hoy no tengo nada claras. Precisamente por eso me importan. Los escribió una versión de mí que todavía no sabía lo que iba a pasar después. No son recuerdos reconstruidos: son mensajes enviados desde un presente que ya no existe.

Lo extraño es que haya decidido volver justo ahora, cuando escribir texto se ha vuelto casi gratis.

Una inteligencia artificial puede proponer una estructura, encontrar argumentos, ofrecer contraejemplos, corregir el tono y devolver en pocos segundos una versión aparentemente clara de casi cualquier cosa. Pelotear con una IA es una forma extraordinaria de explorar una idea. Puedes lanzarle una intuición todavía torpe y recibir preguntas, conexiones y objeciones que quizá habrías tardado días en encontrar.

Pero esa facilidad también introduce una confusión nueva. Leer una idea bien formulada y reconocerse en ella no es lo mismo que haberla pensado. La fluidez produce una falsa sensación de claridad. Es muy fácil terminar una conversación con una IA sintiendo que uno ha llegado a una conclusión cuando, en realidad, solo ha asistido a una conversación convincente.

Por eso creo que en la era de la IA es más importante que nunca sintetizar a mano los propios pensamientos. Pelotear primero, sí. Abrir posibilidades, discutir, dejar que la máquina haga preguntas incómodas. Pero después hay que cerrar el chat y decidir qué queda. Qué afirmación harías tuya. Qué matiz no quieres perder. Qué contradicción sigue sin resolverse.

La IA puede expandir el espacio de lo posible. La última compresión me corresponde a mí. Si no hago ese trabajo, no sé si he pensado algo o si simplemente he reconocido como familiar una buena respuesta.

Estas mismas ideas han peloteado con una IA antes de llegar aquí. No me parece una contradicción. Puede ayudarme a ordenar, recortar o encontrar una frase más precisa. Lo que no puede decidir por mí es qué merece ser recordado. No me preocupa que una máquina me ayude a escribir mejor; me preocuparía llegar a los setenta, leer mis textos y no saber dónde terminaban sus palabras y empezaba realmente mi pensamiento.

En ese sentido, el blog vuelve a ser importante no a pesar de que ahora sobren las palabras, sino precisamente porque sobran. Necesito un lugar en el que una conversación deje de ser un borrador infinito y se convierta en una posición. Un sitio donde decir: después de todas las preguntas y todas las respuestas posibles, esto es lo que hoy creo.

Porque escribir es pensar. Obligar a una intuición a tomar la forma de una frase exige elegir. Cada frase elimina alguna ambigüedad. Cada párrafo establece que una cosa viene después de otra y que, por algún motivo, están relacionadas.

Y escribir también ayuda a construir el relato interno con el que damos sentido a nuestra vida. Las vidas no vienen con una trama. Acumulan trabajos, amores, pérdidas, mudanzas, casualidades y decisiones que solo después intentamos conectar. Al escribir elegimos unas causas, descartamos otras y dibujamos una continuidad entre personas que, aunque compartan nombre, a veces se parecen muy poco.

Tal vez todo ese sentido sea solo un *trucco*, por decirlo como Sorrentino: un artificio que nos contamos para poder vivir dentro de nuestra propia historia. Pero algunos artificios no falsean la vida. La hacen legible.

Y luego está Esteban.

Ahora tiene cinco meses y todavía no puede leer nada. Pero me gustaría que algún día pudiera conocerme de una forma que a mí me habría gustado conocer a mis padres. Me encantaría leer un texto escrito por ellos cuando tenían treinta y seis años, antes de saber cómo terminarían muchas de las historias que yo ya conozco. Saber qué les preocupaba, qué entendían entonces por tener éxito, qué cosas creían haber resuelto y cuáles ni siquiera sabían que estaban a punto de empezar.

Las fotografías me permiten verlos jóvenes. Un texto así me permitiría escucharlos pensar.

No quiero escribir para explicarle a Esteban cómo tiene que vivir ni para dejarle una colección de lecciones. Me basta con ofrecerle materia prima: que pueda conocer a su padre más allá del papel de padre, encontrarse con mis dudas y ver cómo intentaba dar sentido a las cosas mientras ocurrían. Que pueda leer a la persona que yo era cuando él todavía no podía recordarme.

Quizá no lo lea nunca. Tampoco pasa nada. El primer destinatario sigue siendo ese hombre de setenta años que espero llegar a ser.

A los catorce escribía para la gente que había al otro lado de internet. A los treinta y seis escribo para un hombre de setenta y para un niño de cinco meses. Ninguno de los dos puede contestarme hoy. Curiosamente, eso hace que escribir vuelva a parecerme mucho más libre.

Y, de paso, escribir públicamente sigue siendo soltar un mensaje en una botella. Puede recogerlo alguien a quien ya conozco y abrir una conversación que todavía no habíamos tenido. Quizá lo encuentre una persona nueva, se reconozca en alguna idea y acabemos conectando, como ya me ha ocurrido tantas veces.

Ya no necesito que la botella vuelva con una respuesta para justificar haberla lanzado. Pero quiero seguir dejando abierta esa posibilidad.

Durante veinte años escribí para que pasaran cosas. Y pasaron: ligué, gané dinero e hice amigos.

Ahora vuelvo a escribir para que lo que pasa, y lo que pienso mientras pasa, no desaparezca.

I have been writing on the internet since 2004. I was fourteen years old and I started with a blog about my high school. At that age, that was almost the same as making a blog about the whole world.

Over the years the topics and places changed, but the motivation did not change much. I wrote about photography in Xataka Foto. Then I had a photoblog in El País. All that happened while I was in college. Later I published a few articles on Medium, but for a long time my real blog was Twitter. I split thousands of ideas into smaller and smaller pieces, until I gathered more than 30,000 people on the other side.

Now I see it quite clearly. I always wrote so that someone would do something.

I wanted people to read my work, of course, but not out of a noble calling to contribute to the public conversation. I wrote because I needed to get dates, make money and make friends. I could make those reasons sound noble now, but that is the truth. And it is also true that I achieved all three things.

Writing publicly led me, directly or indirectly, to meet my wife, many of my current best friends and practically every single one of the dozens of people I have hired over these years at Graphext. Seen this way, writing on the internet has not been an accessory of my adult life. It has been one of its invisible infrastructures.

There was also another motivation, something harder to explain. I wrote to force myself to have a more interesting life. If you want to have something to tell, you have to pay more attention, move and go out to find it. A blog was a kind of contract with the version of myself I wanted to be. First you build a character, and then you try to live up to it.

I think it worked. I do not know how many things I did because I really wanted to do them and how many because I sensed that one day I could tell them. The difference probably does not matter much. The story also pushed the life.

I wrote outwards. And that forced me to live outwards.

Now I am thirty-six years old. I am married, Esteban was born five months ago and I am doing very well professionally. It does not mean that I no longer want to be liked, make more money or meet interesting people. It means that that engine no longer pulls me with the same force. For the first time, writing again does not respond to a strategy or an urgent need for something to happen on the other side of the screen.

I want to write so I can read myself when I am seventy years old.

Writing for that future reader also solves a problem that I notice more and more as I get older. Many times I discard an idea before writing it because it does not seem very original to me. Surely someone has already thought of it, explained it better and written a book about it. Then I decide that it is not worth adding another worse version to the internet.

Something similar happens to me with cinema. I have the feeling of having already seen all the narrative tropes of all the movies. A character appears and I think I know what arc they will have. A scene begins and I immediately remember others from which it seems to descend. Accumulating references helps to understand things better, but it can also become a machine to take away their value. Since I recognize the ingredients, I assume that the dish can no longer surprise me.

If I write for myself, originality stops being the price of admission. The seventy-year-old man who reads this will not care if the thirty-six-year-old was the first to think of an idea. He will want to know which ones mattered to him, how he reached them and what he did with them. A thought does not have to be unpublished to deserve to be kept. It is enough that it is truly mine at this moment.

That gives me back a motivation to write that I had been losing. I do not have to provide a great new idea every time I publish. I can try to understand an old idea on my own. In thirty years, the valuable thing will not be having been original, but having left an honest trail.

That does not turn a public blog into a private diary. As I get older I have learned that not everything that happens to me belongs entirely to me. A family argument, a friend's bad moment or a tension with a coworker are part of my life, but also of theirs. They have not chosen to become supporting characters in my story.

That is why I now value self-censorship much more. The word has a bad reputation because it sounds like fear or a lack of sincerity, but sometimes it is a form of care and loyalty. In the heat of a moment, a temporary intimacy can seem essential to explain what one feels. A few months later it may have been resolved, it may have lost all importance or we may discover that we told it in a deeply unfair way. The published text, however, remains.

I think, for example, of the suicide of a friend. I believe he would not have minded if I wrote about it. But the story of his death does not belong only to him and, of course, it does not belong only to me. It is also part of the grief and intimacy of his family and the friends who loved him. Telling it could help me sort out what I felt. Publishing it could force them to encounter a version of something they might prefer to live outside the internet.

There is the difference between writing and publishing. I may need to write a story without having the right to share it.

Being honest about what I think does not give me the right to expose the intimacy of my family, my friends or my coworkers. I want to write with enough depth to preserve my thoughts, but also with enough caution not to fix others in a moment that was only temporary. There are silences that are not cowardice. They are affection.

The texts I wrote twenty years ago move me in a way that the photographs, videos or tweets from back then do not achieve. A photo preserves what was in front of it. A video keeps how we moved and how our voice sounded. A tweet preserves a remark or a reaction. But a long text keeps something different. It keeps the path my head took to get from one idea to another.

Many of those texts seem naive to me. Some are poorly written. In others I discover someone too sure of things that today I am not clear about at all. That is exactly why they matter to me. A version of me who did not yet know what was going to happen next wrote them. They are not reconstructed memories. They are messages sent from a present that no longer exists.

The strange thing is that I have decided to return right now, when writing text has become almost free.

An artificial intelligence can propose a structure, find arguments, offer counterexamples, correct the tone and return in a few seconds an apparently clear version of almost anything. Bouncing ideas with an AI is an extraordinary way to explore an idea. You can throw a still clumsy intuition at it and receive questions, connections and objections that you might have taken days to find.

But that ease also introduces a new confusion. Reading a well-formulated idea and recognizing oneself in it is not the same as having thought it. Fluency produces a false sense of clarity. It is very easy to end a conversation with an AI feeling that one has reached a conclusion when, in reality, one has only attended a convincing conversation.

That is why I believe that in the age of AI it is more important than ever to synthesize one's own thoughts by hand. Bounce ideas first, yes. Open possibilities, discuss, let the machine ask uncomfortable questions. But then you have to close the chat and decide what remains. What statement you would make yours. What nuance you do not want to lose. What contradiction remains unresolved.

AI can expand the space of what is possible. The final compression belongs to me. If I do not do that work, I do not know if I have thought something or if I have simply recognized a good answer as familiar.

These same ideas have bounced with an AI before arriving here. It does not seem like a contradiction to me. It can help me sort, trim or find a more precise sentence. What it cannot decide for me is what deserves to be remembered. I do not worry that a machine helps me write better. I would worry about reaching seventy, reading my texts and not knowing where its words ended and my thoughts really began.

In that sense, the blog becomes important again not despite the fact that there are now too many words, but precisely because there are too many. I need a place where a conversation stops being an infinite draft and becomes a position. A place to say that after all the questions and all the possible answers, this is what I believe today.

Because writing is thinking. Forcing an intuition to take the form of a sentence requires choosing. Each sentence eliminates some ambiguity. Each paragraph establishes that one thing comes after another and that, for some reason, they are related.

And writing also helps to build the internal story with which we give meaning to our life. Lives do not come with a plot. They accumulate jobs, loves, losses, moves, coincidences and decisions that we only try to connect later. By writing we choose some causes, discard others and draw a continuity between people who, although they share a name, sometimes look very little alike.

Perhaps all that meaning is just a *trucco*, to say it like Sorrentino. It is an artifice that we tell ourselves to be able to live inside our own story. But some artifices do not falsify life. They make it readable.

And then there is Esteban.

Now he is five months old and he still cannot read anything. But I would like him to be able to know me one day in a way that I would have liked to know my parents. I would love to read a text written by them when they were thirty-six years old, before knowing how many of the stories that I already know would end. I would like to know what worried them, what they understood then by being successful, what things they thought they had solved and which ones they did not even know were about to start.

Photographs allow me to see them young. A text like that would allow me to hear them think.

I do not want to write to explain to Esteban how he has to live or to leave him a collection of lessons. It is enough for me to offer him raw material. I want him to be able to know his father beyond the role of father, encounter my doubts and see how I tried to make sense of things as they happened. I want him to be able to read the person I was when he still could not remember me.

Maybe he will never read it. That is fine too. The first recipient is still that seventy-year-old man I hope to become.

At fourteen I wrote for the people on the other side of the internet. At thirty-six I write for a seventy-year-old man and for a five-month-old boy. Neither of them can answer me today. Curiously, that makes writing seem much freer to me again.

And, by the way, writing publicly is still dropping a message in a bottle. Someone I already know can pick it up and open a conversation we had not had yet. Maybe a new person will find it, recognize themselves in some idea and we will end up connecting, as has already happened to me so many times.

I no longer need the bottle to return with an answer to justify having thrown it. But I want to keep that possibility open.

For twenty years I wrote so that things would happen. And they happened. I got dates, I made money and I made friends.

Now I write again so that what happens, and what I think while it happens, does not disappear.

> Desde el sesgo de un informático que trabaja haciendo un producto para que las empresas analicen sus datos

![](/api/images/blog/2019/6/8/informatica-o-matematicas-que-carrera-estudiar-si-te-quieres-dedicar-al-mundo-de-los-datos/image-01.png "text-width")

Una de las diapositivas que suelo usar en nuestra presentación de [Graphext](http://www.graphext.com/) para inversores

A raíz de [un tweet](https://twitter.com/victorianoi/status/1134367301703282688) que escribí el otro día,

[Guillermo](https://medium.com/u/69db7ad5ef9c?source=post_page-----62670c465e40--------------------------------)

saca en El Confidencial

[un artículo sobre el tema](https://www.elconfidencial.com/tecnologia/2019-06-08/estudiar-matematicas-carrera-selectividad-big-data-empleo_2060062/)

y como no me dio tiempo ayer a hablar con él, aquí recopilo los principales puntos de cómo veo

**lo que se aprende en las carreras**

vs

**qué demanda el mercado laboral**

:

## **¿Qué tipo de persona eres?**

Si en el instituto pensabas que las mates eran algo mucho más grande, elegante y potente que lo que te enseñaban en clase y te aburrían, memorizar procedimientos para calcular cosas en vez de aprender a **representar fenómenos del mundo real en números**, vectores, operaciones y funciones que puede resolver problemas del mundo real… Si has leído por tu cuenta algún libro sobre mates o física, si tus padres son profes de matemáticas y lo vienes mamando desde niño, y si ya sabes algo de programación y le ves el puntillo…

entonces quizás sea muy buena idea que estudies **matemáticas** y si tienes capacidad de trabajo prueba con el doble grado con Informática. Podrás llegar a avanzar este campo, **investigar en la Universidad** o en empresas punteras como Deepmind de Google o en startups chulas como

[Graphext](https://medium.com/u/e97dd5c6a8ed?source=post_page-----62670c465e40--------------------------------)

.

Si en el instituto le veías el punto a las mates pero eres una persona muy curiosa, te interesa un poco todo y más **pragmático**, necesitas ver resultados a corto para motivarte y ansías tener autonomía (incluso algún día montar tu propia empresa) entonces quizás es mejor que hagas informática.

Creo que para ser feliz en una profesión **te tienes que sentir bueno** en ella y para ello tienes que tener la motivación de entender bien para qué sirve y poder tener pequeñas recompensas (y la informática es mucho más agradecida que las Matemáticas o Física)

## **El mercado laboral del análisis de datos**

# ¿Qué se hace realmente hoy día con datos en la mayoría de empresas?

## **Los Data Engineers**

Básicamente **juntar datos** que están esparcidos por diversas bases de datos, limpiarlos y aplicar funciones de **agregación sencillas** con queries en SQL, Python o [map reduce](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/MapReduce) con Spark en los casos más avanzados. A estos perfiles se les llama ***data engineers*** y cobran bastante bien. De esto no te van a enseñar nada o casi nada en la carrera de Matemáticas, en Informática sí.

## **Los Business Analysts**

Luego sen **visualizan esto datos en un **[**dashboard**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dashboard_(business))** **para ver tendencias en gráficos de barras y líneas. Las empresas tochas puede que quieran hacerse esto muy customizado y para ello necesitan programadores (no matemáticos), otras usarán herramientas de *Business Intelligence*, tipo [Tableau](https://www.tableau.com/), Qlik o Power BI y para eso no hace falta ni saber programar.

Para interpretar esos dashboards pero sobre todo **para diseñarlos** hacen falta buenas nociones de estadística pero eso es algo que fácilmente puede aprender ***cualquier ingeniero, estadístico*** incluso gente que proviene de ciertas carreras de ***ciencias sociales***, ADE, Económicas…

Con esa base creo que es más suficiente, lo que te diferenciará aquí en el mercado será **la experiencia que ganes interpretando datos de nichos** (financieros de un banco, de marketing de retornos en inversión publicitaria, datos electorales etc) pero no necesitas estudiar Mates.

Antes esta gente básicamente eran los frikis del Excel, ahora usan herramientas que ingieren más volumen de datos y son más flexibles pintando gráficos para hacer informes/presentaciones de estadística descriptiva en Powerpoint. A esta gente se llama en inglés “***Business Analysts***”

y son muy demandados (de todos los perfiles que comento probablemente sea del que encuentres más ofertas abiertas) tanto en consultoría como en cualquier empresa medio grande. Ahora mismo en Madrid puede haber perfectamente más de 20–30 masters/programas entre centros públicos y privados formando gente para analizar datos a ese nivel. Así que cada vez hay más competencia también. Ganan entre 25K (junior) a 40–50K (seniors)

## **Los Data Scientists**

Luego están los “***data scientists***” que son los que hacen cosas más allá de estadística descriptiva sobre los KPIs (variables que indican cómo va el negocio), estos más que describir los datos aspiran a **crear modelos** (que combinan muchas variables) para **predecir el futuro.**

![](/api/images/blog/2019/6/8/informatica-o-matematicas-que-carrera-estudiar-si-te-quieres-dedicar-al-mundo-de-los-datos/image-02.png "text-width")

Otra slide del deck de inversores de [Graphext](http://www.graphext.com/)

Esto perfiles también están muy demandados, pero la realidad es que **muy pocas empresas en España tienen grandes equipos data science**. Todo el IBEX dice tenerlos pero la mayoría subcontrata consultoras tipo McKinsey, BCG…sólo bancos y telecos tienen más de 10 personas por equipo.

Además hay herramientas que están automatizando y haciéndoles más productivos como nuestro [@graphext](https://twitter.com/graphext) ;) [@DataRobo](https://twitter.com/DataRobot)t ,

[H2O.ai](https://medium.com/u/9aea625dfc27?source=post_page-----62670c465e40--------------------------------)

Crear modelos para predecir qué clientes tienen más posibilidad de irse o cuánto stock necesitan las tiendas **ahora es un poco artesanal pero dejará de serlo.**

Ahora mismo usar [Xgboost](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_boosting) o cualquier algoritmo es usar una librería de Python y jugar a tunear parámetros y tratar las variables para que funcione mejor. Obviamente saber mates ayuda pero **un informático no debería tener tanto problema en aprenderlo rápido** (en muchas especialidades será de hecho parte de currículum) y además tendrá más capacidad de que el código que escriba se pueda integrar en todo el sistema de la empresa sin que necesiten contratar a otra persona más. También puedes aprender data science por tu cuenta haciendo cursos de [Coursera](https://www.coursera.org/courses?query=andrew+ng) o viendo vídeos de [Jaime Altozano](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OE4gcdjFbmc).

Si para un banco optimizar ese algoritmo unas décimas para dar créditos tiene un impacto económico fuerte puede que le venga bien tener unos matemáticos que entiendan todo muy muy a fondo pero no necesita más de 1 o 2, necesitan muchos más ingenieros.

Además si has estudiado informática y te pica la curiosidad de las tripas matemáticas siempre podrás hacer masters en matemáticas y tendrás muchas más intuiciones ganadas (aunque lo más probable es que ya ganes bien, tengas pareja y poco tiempo y no lo acabes haciendo) :P

de hecho **la mayoría de grandes mentes que están avanzando el mundo de data science hoy día han estudiado informática **como [@demishassabis](https://twitter.com/demishassabis) , [@ylecun](https://twitter.com/ylecun) , [Mikolov](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=oBu8kMMAAAAJ&hl=en), [Leskovec](https://www.linkedin.com/in/leskovec/), [@AndrewYNg](https://twitter.com/AndrewYNg) , [@JeffDean](https://twitter.com/JeffDean) , [@alexjc](https://twitter.com/alexjc) mirad sus Linkedins. Antiguamente los que avanzaron el campo eran principalmente matemáticos y físicos porque no existía Informática.

Saber matemáticas al final son **intuiciones** sobre cómo operar con vectores de números y combinatoria, algo que **los informáticos desarrollamos mucho más rápido con nuestro lenguaje que nos da feedback constante** y no con pizarras con jeroglíficos. En esta charla [Conrad Wolfram lo explica muy bien.](https://www.ted.com/talks/conrad_wolfram_teaching_kids_real_math_with_computers/transcript?utm_campaign=&utm_content=addthis-custom&utm_medium=on.ted.com-twitter&utm_source=t.co&awesm=on.ted.com_f7jm&language=es)

por eso** casi siempre recomendaría estudiar Informática en vez de Mates (solas)**.

Por favor **el mundo necesita muchísimos más informáticos e informáticas**, montones de ideas maravillosas para todos los sectores (salud, financieros, transporte, educación) que no se hacen por falta de gente.

Todos estos puestos de trabajo están muy bien pagados, raro sería que ganaras menos de **40K** al año en cualquiera de ellos (que comparado con el resto de profesiones es un sueldazo en España). Además muchas empresas dan mucha **flexibilidad** y te dejarán trabajar **en remoto** desde provincias sin tener que mudarte a Madrid o Barcelona. Y cada vez iremos viendo más data scientists, data engineeers que pasen de los **60K** (que ahora mismo diría que es el techo de cristal) y ganarán más que muchos managers.

> From the bias of a computer scientist who works making a product for companies to analyze their data

![](/api/images/blog/2019/6/8/informatica-o-matematicas-que-carrera-estudiar-si-te-quieres-dedicar-al-mundo-de-los-datos/image-01.png "text-width")

One of the slides I usually use in our [Graphext](http://www.graphext.com/) presentation for investors

Following [a tweet](https://twitter.com/victorianoi/status/1134367301703282688) I wrote the other day,

[Guillermo](https://medium.com/u/69db7ad5ef9c?source=post_page-----62670c465e40--------------------------------)

publishes in El Confidencial

[an article about the topic](https://www.elconfidencial.com/tecnologia/2019-06-08/estudiar-matematicas-carrera-selectividad-big-data-empleo_2060062/)

and since I did not have time yesterday to talk with him, here I collect the main points of how I see

**what you learn in degrees**

vs

**what the job market demands**

:

## **What kind of person are you?**

If in high school you thought math was something much bigger, elegant and powerful than what they taught you in class and you were bored, memorizing procedures to calculate things instead of learning to **represent real world phenomena in numbers**, vectors, operations and functions that can solve real world problems... If you have read on your own a book about math or physics, if your parents are math teachers and you have absorbed it since you were a child, and if you already know some programming and you see the appeal...

then maybe it is a very good idea that you study **mathematics** and if you have the capacity for work try the double degree with Computer Science. You will be able to advance this field, **research at the University** or in leading companies like Google Deepmind or in cool startups like

[Graphext](https://medium.com/u/e97dd5c6a8ed?source=post_page-----62670c465e40--------------------------------)

.

If in high school you saw the point of math but you are a very curious person, you are interested in a bit of everything and more **pragmatic**, you need to see short term results to motivate yourself and you crave autonomy (even one day starting your own company) then maybe it is better that you do computer science.

I think that to be happy in a profession **you have to feel good** at it and for that you must have the motivation to understand well what it is for and be able to have small rewards (and computer science is much more rewarding than Mathematics or Physics)

## **The job market of data analysis**

# What is really done today with data in most companies?

## **The Data Engineers**

Basically **joining data** that is scattered across various databases, cleaning it and applying **simple aggregation** functions with queries in SQL, Python or [map reduce](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/MapReduce) with Spark in the most advanced cases. These profiles are called ***data engineers*** and they earn quite well. They will not teach you anything or almost anything about this in the Mathematics degree, in Computer Science they will.

## **The Business Analysts**

Then they **visualize this data in a **[**dashboard**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dashboard_(business))** **to see trends in bar and line charts. Big companies might want to make this very customized and for that they need programmers (not mathematicians), others will use *Business Intelligence* tools, like [Tableau](https://www.tableau.com/), Qlik or Power BI and for that you do not even need to know how to program.

To interpret those dashboards but above all **to design them** you need good notions of statistics but that is something that ***any engineer, statistician*** can easily learn, even people who come from certain ***social sciences*** degrees, Business Administration, Economics...

With that base I think it is more than enough, what will differentiate you here in the market will be **the experience you gain interpreting niche data** (financials of a bank, marketing returns on advertising investment, electoral data etc) but you do not need to study Math.

Before these people were basically the Excel geeks, now they use tools that ingest more data volume and are more flexible painting charts to make descriptive statistics reports/presentations in Powerpoint. These people are called in English "***Business Analysts***"

and they are in high demand (of all the profiles I mention it is probably the one you find the most open offers for) both in consulting and in any medium large company. Right now in Madrid there can perfectly be more than 20 to 30 masters/programs between public and private centers training people to analyze data at that level. So there is also more and more competition. They earn between 25K (junior) to 40 to 50K (seniors)

## **The Data Scientists**

Then there are the "***data scientists***" who are the ones who do things beyond descriptive statistics on the KPIs (variables that indicate how the business is doing), these rather than describing the data aspire to **create models** (that combine many variables) to **predict the future.**

![](/api/images/blog/2019/6/8/informatica-o-matematicas-que-carrera-estudiar-si-te-quieres-dedicar-al-mundo-de-los-datos/image-02.png "text-width")

Another slide from the investor deck of [Graphext](http://www.graphext.com/)

These profiles are also in high demand, but the reality is that **very few companies in Spain have large data science teams**. All the IBEX says they have them but most subcontract consulting firms like McKinsey, BCG... only banks and telcos have more than 10 people per team.

Besides there are tools that are automating and making them more productive like our [@graphext](https://twitter.com/graphext) ;) [@DataRobo](https://twitter.com/DataRobot)t ,

[H2O.ai](https://medium.com/u/9aea625dfc27?source=post_page-----62670c465e40--------------------------------)

Creating models to predict which customers have more possibility of leaving or how much stock stores need **is now a bit artisanal but it will stop being so.**

Right now using [Xgboost](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_boosting) or any algorithm is using a Python library and playing to tune parameters and treat the variables so it works better. Obviously knowing math helps but **a computer scientist should not have so much problem learning it fast** (in many specialties it will in fact be part of the curriculum) and besides they will have more capacity so that the code they write can be integrated into the whole system of the company without them needing to hire another person. You can also learn data science on your own by doing [Coursera](https://www.coursera.org/courses?query=andrew+ng) courses or watching videos by [Jaime Altozano](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OE4gcdjFbmc).

If for a bank optimizing that algorithm a few tenths to give credits has a strong economic impact it might be good for them to have some mathematicians who understand everything very very deeply but they do not need more than 1 or 2, they need many more engineers.

Besides if you have studied computer science and the mathematical guts pique your curiosity you can always do masters in mathematics and you will have many more gained intuitions (although the most probable thing is that you already earn well, have a partner and little time and you do not end up doing it) :P

in fact **most of the great minds that are advancing the world of data science today have studied computer science **like [@demishassabis](https://twitter.com/demishassabis) , [@ylecun](https://twitter.com/ylecun) , [Mikolov](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=oBu8kMMAAAAJ&hl=en), [Leskovec](https://www.linkedin.com/in/leskovec/), [@AndrewYNg](https://twitter.com/AndrewYNg) , [@JeffDean](https://twitter.com/JeffDean) , [@alexjc](https://twitter.com/alexjc) look at their Linkedins. In the past those who advanced the field were mainly mathematicians and physicists because Computer Science did not exist.

Knowing mathematics in the end are **intuitions** about how to operate with vectors of numbers and combinatorics, something that **we computer scientists develop much faster with our language that gives us constant feedback** and not with blackboards with hieroglyphs. In this talk [Conrad Wolfram explains it very well.](https://www.ted.com/talks/conrad_wolfram_teaching_kids_real_math_with_computers/transcript?utm_campaign=&utm_content=addthis-custom&utm_medium=on.ted.com-twitter&utm_source=t.co&awesm=on.ted.com_f7jm&language=es)

that is why** I would almost always recommend studying Computer Science instead of Math (alone)**.

Please **the world needs many more computer scientists**, lots of wonderful ideas for all sectors (health, financial, transport, education) that are not done due to lack of people.

All these jobs are very well paid, it would be rare for you to earn less than **40K** a year in any of them (which compared to the rest of professions is a huge salary in Spain). Besides many companies give a lot of **flexibility** and will let you work **remotely** from provinces without having to move to Madrid or Barcelona. And we will increasingly see more data scientists, data engineers who pass **60K** (which right now I would say is the glass ceiling) and they will earn more than many managers.

---

*15 mil personas participaron en *[*un meme de Twitter*](https://twitter.com/search?q=%22First+language%22+AND+%22difficulties%22&src=typed_query&f=live)* donde se les pedía expresar su relación con los lenguajes de programación.*

*Recopilamos y analizamos con *[*Graphext*](http://www.graphext.com/)* todas las respuestas. Aquí están las principales conclusiones que encontré.*

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-01.jpg "text-width")

Cada nodo es una persona y su tuit, aquellos que **respondieron de forma más similar se conectan **([Graphext](http://www.graphext.com/) y su algoritmo de reducción de dimensionalidad calculan una puntuación de similitud). En los extremos encuentras personas que mencionaron el mismo lenguaje para todas las categorías, como

[Ryan Florence](https://medium.com/u/162352c45b6e?source=post_page-----4f7ae105e843--------------------------------)

La pregunta que más se correlaciona con el resto es sobre cuál es el lenguaje de programación más usado. En la imagen podemos ver un mapa claro de **desarrolladores web a la derecha** (Javascript, PHP, Ruby) y **científicos de datos** a la **izquierda** (R, Python) y **C/C++, Java en el medio**.

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-02.jpg "text-width")

Entre los lenguajes de programación más **amados**, **Python le gana al más usado, Javascript**. En el top 10 podemos encontrar 2 lenguajes menos usados pero emergentes que ya tienen muchos fans: **Go** y **Rust.**

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-03.jpg "text-width")

Cuando vemos el ranking de los **lenguajes de programación más odiados** y su distribución, queda claro que** casi todo el mundo odia Java** sin importar qué otros lenguajes usen más. **Javascript** es odiado principalmente por los que no son desarrolladores web, pero también por personas que lo usan todo el tiempo.

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-04.jpg "text-width")

**Python** gana por goleada cuando se trata de recomendar un lenguaje **para principiantes **para casi todos los programadores, excepto para los desarrolladores web que se decantan por Javascript. **Ruby** es bastante recomendado en relación a su uso.

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-05.jpg "text-width")

**Basic, Pascal, QBASIC, Visual Basic**… destacan como los lenguajes de programación que **aprendieron primero** las personas que participaron en el meme de la encuesta colaborativa. Pero **ninguno de estos lenguajes se recomienda hoy en día** para aprender a programar.

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-06.jpg "text-width")

Los lenguajes de programación que** dan más dolores de cabeza** son **C** y **C ++** y se decantan por Python. Muchos de los que usan Javascript tienen algún **trauma con Java**. Hay muchos que alucinan con la **programación funcional** (**Haskell**, Lisp) o con la declarativa (**Prolog**) o con **Ensamblador** en la universidad.

*15K thousand people participated in *[*a Twitter meme*](https://twitter.com/search?q=%22First+language%22+AND+%22difficulties%22&src=typed_query&f=live)* where they were asked to express their relationship with programming languages.*

*We collected and analyzed with *[*Graphext*](http://www.graphext.com/)* all the answers. Here are the main insights that I found.*

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-01.jpg "text-width")

Each node is a person and their tweet, those who **answered more similarly get connected **([Graphext](http://www.graphext.com/) dimensionality reduction algorithm calculate a similarity score) In the extremes you find people that mentioned the same language for all the categories), like

[Ryan Florence](https://medium.com/u/162352c45b6e?source=post_page-----4f7ae105e843--------------------------------)

The question that correlates more with the rest of is about what is the programming language is more used. In the image we can see a clear map of **web developers on the right** (Javascript, PHP, Ruby) and **data scientists** on the **left** (R, Python) and **C/C++, Java in the middle**.

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-02.jpg "text-width")

Among the most **loved** programming languages, **Python wins over the most used, Javascript**. In the top 10 we can find 2 less used languages but emerging with many fans already: **Go** and **Rust.**

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-03.jpg "text-width")

When we see the ranking of the **most hated programming languages** and their distribution, it’s clear that** almost everybody hates Java** no matter what other languages they use the most. **Javascript** is mostly hated among non web developers but also by people that use it all the time.

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-04.jpg "text-width")

**Python** wins by far when it comes to recommending a language **for beginners **for almost most programmers, except for web developers that go for Javascript. **Ruby** is quite recommended relatively respect to its usage.

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-05.jpg "text-width")

**Basic, Pascal, QBASIC, Visual Basic**… stand out as programming languages that were **learnt first** by the people who participated in the crowdsourced survey meme. But **none of these languages are recommended today** to learn programming.

![](/api/images/blog/2019/10/12/analyzing-the-complex-relationship-between-the-most-loved-hated-and-used-programming-languages/image-06.jpg "text-width")

The programming languages that** give more headaches** are **C** and **C ++** and they go for Python. Many who use Javascript have some **trauma with Java**. There are many those who freak out with **functional programming** (**Haskell**, Lisp) or with declarative (**Prolog**) or **Assembly** in college.

title: "Probando la cámara del nuevo iPhone 13 Pro"
slug: "2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada"
description: "Salí a pasear por Granada con el nuevo iPhone 13 Pro y fotografié todo en Apple ProRAW para comprobar hasta dónde ha llegado la fotografía móvil frente a las cámaras réflex."
locale: es
format: markdown
---

Salí a pasear por [Granada](/es/granada), España, con el nuevo iPhone 13 Pro, presentado la semana anterior. Hice todas las fotografías en formato [Apple ProRAW](https://support.apple.com/es-es/HT211965) para comprobar hasta dónde ha llegado la fotografía digital frente a las cámaras réflex. También utilicé [VSCO](https://vsco.co) para ajustar el color, el brillo y otros parámetros.

![El nuevo zoom óptico 3x, equivalente a un 77 mm, cambia por completo la fotografía documental](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8578.jpg "caption")

![El bosque de la Alhambra, en mi ciudad natal, es uno de los lugares más mágicos del mundo. La luz del atardecer entre los árboles y la antigua fortaleza es delicada y siempre difícil de capturar.](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8538.jpg "caption")

Tengo que decir que estoy **bastante sorprendido con los resultados**, después de haber usado un iPhone XS durante los tres años anteriores. Las mejoras principales respecto a mi antiguo iPhone son:

- El **zoom óptico 3x**. Muchas de mis mejores fotografías callejeras con réflex están hechas con objetivos de 24-105 mm. El zoom 3x equivale a un 77 mm y acabé utilizándolo constantemente para acercar elementos dentro del paisaje urbano, como coches y árboles contra los edificios.
- El nuevo **gran angular 0,5x**, equivalente a 13 mm, también resulta muy útil en imágenes en las que quieres exagerar la presencia de una persona, un animal o cualquier otro elemento sin separarlo de su entorno.

![Procesada en VSCO con el ajuste al5](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/C95ADDA9-C7FE-456B-B1BF-3ED0BAD6EB9F.JPG "gallery-2")
![Procesada en VSCO con el ajuste lv03](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8592.jpg "gallery-2")

También incorpora [**un nuevo objetivo macro**](https://www.tomsguide.com/news/iphone-13-pro-macro-camera-is-so-good-that-a-doctors-using-it-for-this) que es estupendo, aunque probablemente sólo lo use de vez en cuando para fotografiar insectos, hojas y otras cosas bonitas. Desde luego no será mi forma principal de hacer fotos. Me cuesta encontrar originalidad en la fotografía macro y, al final, las criaturas pequeñas se parecen bastante entre sí… 😂

Una de las sorpresas más grandes e inesperadas ha sido el formato **Apple ProRAW**. Apple lo presentó a finales del año anterior para el iPhone 12. Después de probarlo con **VSCO**, estoy muy contento con el control que ofrece sobre las luces y las sombras. La experiencia se acerca mucho a trabajar con **Adobe Camera RAW** y con los archivos RAW de mis cámaras **Canon** y **Sony**. Como se ve en las imágenes de arriba y abajo, el rango dinámico en una situación de luz tan complicada es asombroso 🤯. La [reseña de Austin Mann](https://austinmann.com/trek/iphone-13-pro-camera-review-tanzania) explica también sus posibilidades de vídeo.

![Procesada en VSCO con el ajuste lv03](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/FullSizeRender-2.jpg "gallery-2")
![Procesada en VSCO con el ajuste lv03](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8611.jpg "gallery-2")

![IMG_8530.jpg](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8530.jpg "gallery-2")

![Procesada en VSCO con el ajuste lv03](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8602.jpg "gallery-2")
![IMG_8574.jpg](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8574.jpg "gallery-2")

![](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8511.jpg)

![Modo retrato en fotografía callejera, con un bokeh precioso](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/FullSizeRender.jpg "gallery-2")
![IMG_8528.jpg](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8528.jpg "gallery-2")

El **modo retrato** ya existía en mi anterior iPhone, pero en el 13 es aún más rápido y permite utilizarlo con personas o animales en movimiento, algo estupendo para la fotografía callejera. Ese bokeh es fundamental para aislar a los sujetos dentro de su contexto y sigue siendo una de las cualidades que hace especiales a las réflex. La principal limitación es que no funciona con objetos situados a más de dos metros y todavía no admite Apple ProRAW. Aún no es perfecto, pero mejora año tras año.

I went for a walk in [Granada](/granada), Spain, with the new iPhone 13 Pro, released last week, and shot all the pictures using the [Apple ProRAW](https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT211965) format to see how far digital photography is now compared to DSLR cameras. I also used the [VSCO app](https://vsco.co) for adjusting the color, brightness, and other parameters.

![The new x3 optical zoom, equivalent to a 77mm is a game changer for documentary photography](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8578.jpg "caption")

![The forest of the Alhambra in my hometown is one of the most magical places in the world. These lights during the sunset between the trees and the ancient castle are so delicate and always difficult to capture.](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8538.jpg "caption")

I have to say, I am **pretty amazed by the results**, after using an iPhone XS for the past 3 years. The major improvements with respect to my previous iPhone are:

- The **3X optical zoom**. Most of my best street photography pictures with my DSLR are taken with 24-105mm lenses. The 3X optical zoom is equivalent to a 77mm lens. I found myself using it all the time to bring elements closer in city landscapes. Like cars and trees with buildings.
- The new **0.5X wide-angle lens**, equivalent to 13mm, is also handy for some types of images you can really magnify a person, animal, or element to respect their surroundings.

![Processed with VSCO with al5 preset](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/C95ADDA9-C7FE-456B-B1BF-3ED0BAD6EB9F.JPG "gallery-2")
![Processed with VSCO with lv03 preset](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8592.jpg "gallery-2")

There is also [**a new macro lens**](https://www.tomsguide.com/news/iphone-13-pro-macro-camera-is-so-good-that-a-doctors-using-it-for-this) that is amazing too, but I’ll probably use it only from time to time to capture insects, leaves, and other beautiful stuff, but definitely not my primary focus on taking pictures. I feel like it’s difficult to be original with macro photography and small creatures are pretty similar… 😂

But one of my biggest and unexpected surprises has been the new **Apple ProRAW** format. It was introduced at the end of last year for the iPhone 12. After testing it using **VSCO** I am really happy with how much control I get on the highlights and shadows, pretty similar to the experience with **Adobe Camera RAW** and the RAW files from my DSLRs **Canon** and **Sony**. As you can see in the images above and below the dynamic range in this difficult light situation is astonishing 🤯 . Read the [Austin Mann review](https://austinmann.com/trek/iphone-13-pro-camera-review-tanzania) to learn more about the video capabilities.

![Processed with VSCO with lv03 preset](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/FullSizeRender-2.jpg "gallery-2")
![Processed with VSCO with lv03 preset](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8611.jpg "gallery-2")

![IMG_8539.jpg](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8539.jpg "gallery-2")
![IMG_8530.jpg](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8530.jpg "gallery-2")

![Processed with VSCO with lv03 preset](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8602.jpg "gallery-2")
![IMG_8574.jpg](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8574.jpg "gallery-2")

![](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8511.jpg)

![Portrait mode on Street photography, lovely bokeh](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/FullSizeRender.jpg "gallery-2")
![IMG_8528.jpg](/api/images/blog/2021/10/3/testing-iphone-13-pro-in-granada/IMG_8528.jpg "gallery-2")

The **portrait mode** was already on my previous iPhone but on the 13 is even faster and makes possible to use with people or animals moving which is great for street photography. That bokeh is crucial for isolating the subjects around their context and what still make DSLR quite unique. The main drawback is that you can’t do it with any object more than 2 meters away and don’t support the Apple ProRAW form yet. Still not perfect but getting there year after year.

### 🌐 Macrodatos / 💵 Economía / 🚻 Brechas de género \| 👨‍👩‍👦 Crianza

> Las madres, de media, reducen sus ingresos un 25% o más 10 años después de tener un hijo, mientras que los ingresos de los hombres se mantienen prácticamente igual.

[bookmark](https://app.notion.com/p/e78de7840c194f40a0eceb558993e4bc#a558ec4009b645f284104bf07d5ab6fd)

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-01.jpg "text-width")

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-02.jpg "text-width")

Este dato parece bastante **consistente en 2 estudios diferentes** publicados este año por el Banco de España (gráfico de arriba) y un artículo con datos de EE. UU. (gráfico de abajo).

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-03.jpg "text-width")

La tendencia **no cambia mucho para aquellas mujeres con título universitario**, aunque el efecto parece menor.

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-04.jpg "text-width")

¿Por qué? La mayoría de las **mujeres reducen drásticamente sus horas de trabajo después de tener hijos**. Muchas** de ellas empiezan a trabajar a tiempo parcial**, incluso si tienen un título universitario (21% de mujeres frente al 5% de hombres). ¿Es esto una preferencia, o se sienten obligadas por las normas culturales o por sus maridos? Me temo que estos datos no pueden responder a esa pregunta.

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-05.jpg "text-width")

Paradójicamente, ahora hay [**más mujeres formadas y altamente cualificadas en el mercado laboral que hombres**](https://magnet.xataka.com/preguntas-no-tan-frecuentes/hay-mujeres-jovenes-que-hombres-trabajando-profesiones-alta-cualificacion-espana), y **ganan más dinero que los hombres** antes de tener hijos.

### 🌐 Macrodatos / 💵 Economía / 🎩 Los viejos tiempos / 🏡 Vivienda

> La vivienda era mucho más asequible en los años 90 que desde los 2000 en España y el Reino Unido.

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-08.jpg "text-width")

Cuando [tuiteé sobre ello](https://twitter.com/victorianoi/status/1318451187084120064), [Arturo Herrero](https://twitter.com/ArturoHerrero/status/1318591114190999554) y [Javi López](https://twitter.com/javilop/status/1318646873612234757) mencionaron esta página: [wtfhappenedin1971.com](https://wtfhappenedin1971.com/), donde muestran **docenas de gráficos** intentando demostrar el efecto sobre la **inflación** desde 1971, cuando Richard Nixon canceló los [acuerdos de Bretton Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_system), el fin de **la convertibilidad del dólar en oro**. Desde ese momento, todas las monedas nacionales dejaron de tener un ancla. ¡Las monedas fiduciarias podían crearse sin límites!

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-09.jpg "text-width")

Aparentemente, ese cambio creó inflación; los bancos empezaron a disfrutar de tipos de interés bajos. Desde ese momento, los bancos pudieron ofrecer hipotecas largas y caras, **los precios de la vivienda aumentaron,** y **los salarios reales dejaron de aumentar **tanto como solían crecer décadas antes. Pero, como mis conocimientos de macroeconomía son mínimos, no estoy muy seguro de lo precisa que es esta interpretación… :P

**Otra hipótesis que he escuchado es que** la vivienda no es asequible para la mayoría de la gente porque **las grandes ciudades**, como Madrid o Londres, **han aumentado su población rápidamente** en las últimas décadas. Todo el mundo quiere vivir en estas ciudades, justo en el centro, haciendo que estos precios sean mucho más caros y cambiando las medianas medias de todo el territorio.

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-10.png "text-width")

### 🌐 Macrofacts / 💵 Economics / 🚻 Gender Gaps \| 👨‍👩‍👦 Parenting

> Mothers on avg reduce their earnings by 25% or more after 10 years of having a child, while men’s earnings remains pretty much the same.

[bookmark](https://app.notion.com/p/e78de7840c194f40a0eceb558993e4bc#a558ec4009b645f284104bf07d5ab6fd)

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-01.jpg "text-width")

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-02.jpg "text-width")

This fact seems pretty **consistent in 2 different studies** released this year by the Bank of Spain (chart above) and a paper with US data (chart below).

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-03.jpg "text-width")

The trend **doesn't change much for those women with a college degree**, although the effect seems lower.

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-04.jpg "text-width")

Why? Most **women reduce their working hours drastically after having children**. Many** of them start working part-time**, even if they have a college degree (21% of women vs. 5% of men). Is this a preference, or they feel forced by cultural norms or their husbands? I am afraid this data can’t answer that question.

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-05.jpg "text-width")

Paradoxically, there are now [**more educated and highly skilled women in the job market than men**](https://magnet.xataka.com/preguntas-no-tan-frecuentes/hay-mujeres-jovenes-que-hombres-trabajando-profesiones-alta-cualificacion-espana), and **they make more money than men** before having children.

[Victoriano Izquierdo @victorianoiMirando con microdatos de la última EPA en @graphext  las ocupaciones y actividades donde más diferencia hay de hombres y mujeres de 20 a 44 años.  
Ya hay muchas más mujeres jóvenes en España que hombres trabajando en profesiones de alta cualificación...  
Mini-hilo 👇 7:07 PM ∙ Jan 6, 202062Likes54Retweets](https://twitter.com/victorianoi/status/1214262353602187264)

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-06.jpg "text-width")

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-07.jpg "text-width")

I will look for data about if men are starting to reduce their working hours and going for part-time jobs after becoming fathers in some countries and **if women are starting to prioritize their careers over their families**.

The Child Penalty in Spain.](https://www.bde.es/f/webbde/SES/Secciones/Publicaciones/PublicacionesSeriadas/DocumentosOcasionales/20/Files/do2017e.pdf) (July 2020) & [Children and the Remaining Gender Gaps in the Labor Market](https://www.nber.org/papers/w27980) (October 2020)

### 🌐 Macrofacts / 💵 Economics / 🎩 Good Old Days / 🏡 Housing

> Housing was much more affordable in the 90s than since the 2000s in Spain and the UK.

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-08.jpg "text-width")

When [I tweeted about it](https://twitter.com/victorianoi/status/1318451187084120064), [Arturo Herrero](https://twitter.com/ArturoHerrero/status/1318591114190999554) and [Javi López](https://twitter.com/javilop/status/1318646873612234757) mentioned this page: [wtfhappenedin1971.com](https://wtfhappenedin1971.com/), where they show **dozens of charts** trying to prove the effect on **inflation** since 1971, when Richard Nixon canceled the [Bretton Woods agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_system), the end of **the dollar's convertibility to gold**. From that moment, all national currencies stopped having an anchor. Fiat currencies could be created without limits!

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-09.jpg "text-width")

Apparently, that change created inflation; banks started enjoying low-interest rates. From that moment, banks could offer long and expensive mortgages, **housing prices increased,** and **real wages stop increasing **as much as they used to grow decades before. But, since my macroeconomics knowledge is minimal, I am not so sure how accurate this interpretation is… :P

**Another hypothesis I heard, is that** housing is not affordable for most people because **big cities**, like Madrid or London, **have increased their population rapidly** in the last decades. Everybody wants to live in these cities, right in the city center, making these prices way more expensive and changing the entire territory's avg medians.

![](/api/images/blog/2020/11/1/why-women-earn-less-why-houses-are-so-expensive-now-but-werent-for-our-parents-and-more/image-10.png "text-width")
